original_question: Can one prove in a representation-independent way that the geodesic-orbit property of a homogeneous space does not depend on the chosen coset presentation M = G/K or on the chosen Ad(K)-invariant reductive decomposition g = k + m, especially when one wants to show that the space is in no way naturally reductive?
target_in_paper: Section 10's unnumbered open problem about whether the geodesic-orbit property is intrinsic to a homogeneous Riemannian manifold (M,g), rather than depending on a chosen realization M=G/K and a chosen Ad(K)-invariant reductive splitting g=k⊕m; this is why the paper says it often studies G-g.o. spaces. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the core issue the paper flags at the end: the lack of a representation-independent way to treat the geodesic-orbit property. It also correctly notices the nearby stronger theme that, when natural reductivity is involved, one must vary over all possible transitive isometry groups and not just one preferred presentation. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))
missing_details: The paper is in the Riemannian homogeneous setting: (M,g) is a connected homogeneous Riemannian manifold, G is a connected transitive subgroup of the identity component I0(M), K is the isotropy subgroup at a base point o, and the initial notion is 'G-g.o.' rather than an intrinsic g.o. notion. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))

Your draft should say explicitly what 'independence' means: if (M,g) is realized as G/K and also as G0/K0 by connected transitive isometry groups, then the property that every geodesic is an orbit of a one-parameter subgroup should agree across these realizations, regardless of the chosen Ad(K)- or Ad(K0)-invariant reductive decomposition. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))

The paper frames this as an open difficulty, not as an established theorem; the refined question should therefore ask for an intrinsic criterion or proof, not presuppose that such a result is already known. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))

To be stand-alone, the formulation should distinguish the fixed-presentation algebraic criteria in Section 2 from the intrinsic problem in Section 10: the Geodesic Lemma and Corollary 2.3 characterize the G-g.o. property only after choosing a specific reductive decomposition g=k⊕m and metric operator Λ. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))

The phrase 'in no way naturally reductive' has a stronger universal meaning in the paper: one must rule out natural reductivity for every connected transitive isometry group G0 of (M,g) and every Ad(K0)-invariant reductive decomposition g0=k0⊕m0, not merely for one chosen presentation. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))

No ambient ring, field, degree, or nilpotency parameter is part of this paper's target statement; the missing precision is geometric and quantificational, namely the universal quantifiers over all admissible coset presentations and reductive splittings. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))
refined_question: For a connected homogeneous Riemannian manifold (M,g), is there an intrinsic, presentation-independent criterion for the geodesic-orbit property—equivalently, can one show that whether every geodesic of (M,g) is an orbit of a one-parameter subgroup is independent of the chosen realization M=G/K by a connected transitive isometry group G and of the chosen Ad(K)-invariant reductive decomposition g=k⊕m? In particular, can such an intrinsic viewpoint explain why the paper often works with G-g.o. spaces rather than asserting the full g.o. property a priori?
justification: The closest official target is not a theorem or conjecture but the Section 10 open-problems remark that the author finds it hard to show the g.o. property is independent of the coset presentation and reductive splitting, and therefore often formulates results for G-g.o. spaces. Section 2 gives the exact notation behind that remark: Definition 1 makes the geodesic-orbit notion relative to a chosen transitive isometry group G, while Corollary 2.3 supplies only a fixed-presentation algebraic characterization via a reductive decomposition and metric operator. Your draft is therefore close in spirit, but it needs the Riemannian/connected/transitive-isometry hypotheses and the explicit universal quantifiers over all presentations to be fully stand-alone and paper-faithful. The phrase about being 'in no way naturally reductive' is relevant context from Section 3 together with Definitions 3–4, because natural reductivity itself is defined existentially over some transitive isometry group; however, that stronger natural-reductivity issue is motivation around the target, not the paper's official open problem itself. ([maths.tcd.ie](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/ims/bull79/bull79.pdf))
